body:
Language family and origin

Gujarati is a major language of western India belonging to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-Iranian group of the Indo-European language family. It shares a common linguistic ancestry with languages such as Hindi, Marathi, Punjabi, Bengali and Rajasthani.

The name Gujarati is historically associated with Gujarat and the Gurjara people. However, Gujarati did not emerge suddenly when Gujarat acquired its regional identity. It developed gradually through successive changes in the speech of western India.

Evolution from earlier Indo-Aryan languages

The historical development of Gujarati can be understood through the 3 broad stages of Indo-Aryan linguistic history:

  • Old Indo-Aryan: Represented by Vedic Sanskrit and later Sanskrit.
  • Middle Indo-Aryan: Represented by Prakrit languages and their later forms, known as Apabhramsha.
  • New Indo-Aryan: Represented by languages such as Gujarati, Hindi, Marathi and Bengali.

Prakrit refers to a group of historically related Middle Indo-Aryan languages. Apabhramsha refers to later linguistic forms that developed from the Prakrit traditions and contributed to the emergence of New Indo-Aryan languages.

Gujarati developed particularly from the western Apabhramsha tradition associated with Shauraseni Prakrit. The regional form of Apabhramsha associated with Gujarat is commonly called Gurjara Apabhramsha or Nagara Apabhramsha.

Apabhramsha is an important historical link between Prakrit and Gujarati. Modern Gujarati did not develop directly from Classical Sanskrit without intermediate linguistic stages.

Historical stages of Gujarati

Gujarati is conventionally divided into Old Gujarati, Middle Gujarati and Modern Gujarati. These divisions are based on changes in grammar, pronunciation, vocabulary and literary usage.

Old Gujarati

In a commonly used historical classification, Old Gujarati covers approximately 1100–1500 CE. It was closely connected with the linguistic traditions of western Rajasthan. Its literary forms retained several characteristics of Apabhramsha while developing features recognisable in later Gujarati.

Old Gujarati is also associated with the terms Old Western Rajasthani and Maru-Gurjar. These names reflect the shared linguistic heritage of Gujarat and Rajasthan before their languages became more distinctly differentiated.

Middle Gujarati

Middle Gujarati broadly covers 1500–1800 CE in this classification. Gujarati became increasingly distinct from Rajasthani during its historical development. Its vocabulary, grammatical constructions and pronunciation gradually acquired forms closer to those of the modern language.

Modern Gujarati

Modern Gujarati broadly refers to the form of the language used from approximately 1800 CE onwards in this classification. Printing, formal education, newspapers, dictionaries and modern literature contributed to its standardisation and wider public use.

Historical periods are approximate

There is no universally accepted boundary between these stages. Another classification places the Old or Apabhramsha period in the 10th–14th centuries, the Middle period in the 15th–17th centuries and the Modern period after the 17th century. These differences reflect the gradual nature of language change and the criteria used by different scholars.

The historical stages of a language should also be distinguished from the periods of its literature. A literary period may be defined by major authors, movements or forms of writing rather than exclusively by changes in grammar and pronunciation.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarati belongs to the Indo-European language family.
  • Its linguistic branch is Indo-Aryan.
  • Gurjara or Nagara Apabhramsha is an important historical predecessor of Gujarati.
  • Old Western Rajasthani and Maru-Gurjar refer to the shared early linguistic tradition of Gujarat and Rajasthan.
  • Old Gujarati, Middle Gujarati and Modern Gujarati represent successive historical stages.
  • Trap: Gujarati is a New Indo-Aryan language, not a Dravidian language or a surviving Prakrit language.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 7, English edition 2021–22, Chapter 8, Formation of Regional Culture, p. 41; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Gujarat: Gujarati Language and Literature, sections on origin and historical development; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Gujarati, Vol. XI, Fascicle 4, pp. 391–392; Neo-Brahmi Generation Panel, Proposal for a Gujarati Script Root Zone Label Generation Ruleset, 6 March 2019, pp. 2–4. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026. Online state-board textbook copies were used because the corresponding project scans were not readable.]

title: Origin and Historical Development of Gujarati

body:
Acharya Hemachandra and early linguistic evidence

Acharya Hemachandra was a prominent 12th-century Jain scholar, grammarian and literary figure associated with the Chaulukya or Solanki period of Gujarat. He received royal patronage during the reigns of Siddharaja Jayasimha and Kumarapala.

His major grammatical work, Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana, also known as Siddha-Hema, deals with Sanskrit and Prakrit grammar, including Apabhramsha. Its treatment of Apabhramsha and its examples of contemporary linguistic forms provide valuable evidence for understanding the transition towards Gujarati.

The Apabhramsha verses preserved in this grammatical tradition help scholars identify features of the earlier spoken and literary languages of western India.

Hemachandra documented and systematised existing linguistic forms. He did not invent Apabhramsha or create the Gujarati language. Languages evolve through the usage of generations of speakers.

Jain contributions to Old Gujarati

Jain scholars played a major role in the preservation and development of early Gujarati writing. Religious narratives, moral instruction, biographies and commentaries were composed in regional linguistic forms that could reach audiences beyond those familiar with Sanskrit.

Several Jain works from the late 12th century demonstrate the emergence of the literary language commonly identified as Old Gujarati or Maru-Gurjar.

WorkAuthorHistorical association
Bharateshwar Bahubali GhorVajrasena SuriEarly Jain literary tradition; approximate dating
Bharateshwar Bahubali RasShalibhadra Suri1185 CE
Jambusami ChariyaDharmasuri1210 CE

Bharateshwar Bahubali Ras is particularly important because it is one of the earliest securely dated literary compositions associated with Old Gujarati. It narrates the story of Bharata and Bahubali from the Jain tradition.

Earlier and approximately dated works also survive. Therefore, the date 1185 CE represents an important milestone in documented Gujarati literature rather than the date on which Gujarati first came into existence.

Basic features of Old Gujarati

Old Gujarati retained several linguistic features inherited from Apabhramsha while developing grammatical constructions that anticipated the modern language. These included the growing use of postpositions and auxiliary verbs.

A postposition is a grammatical element placed after a noun or pronoun to express a relationship such as possession, location or direction. An auxiliary verb is a verb used to help express tense, aspect or another grammatical meaning.

The increasing use of such constructions was part of the historical movement away from the more extensive system of word endings found in earlier Indo-Aryan languages.

Bhakti literature and the expansion of Gujarati

The spread of the Bhakti tradition encouraged the use of regional languages for religious expression. Devotional compositions in familiar speech could circulate among ordinary people without requiring knowledge of Sanskrit.

Narsinh Mehta, the 15th-century Gujarati devotional poet, occupies a central position in this development. His compositions helped establish Gujarati as an important medium of devotional expression. His well-known devotional song, Vaishnava Jana To, expresses the ideal of compassion towards others.

Narsinh Mehta is traditionally honoured as Adikavi, meaning the first or pioneering poet of Gujarati literature. This literary title should not be interpreted as evidence that no Gujarati compositions existed before him. The Jain literary tradition predates his period.

Bhalan, associated with Patan, contributed to the development of narrative poetry in Gujarati. His use of the expression Gurjar Bhakha is significant in the history of the language because it identifies the regional speech as a recognisable linguistic tradition.

Mirabai's devotional songs also circulated widely in Rajasthan and Gujarat. This illustrates how literary traditions could cross regional linguistic boundaries.

Changes associated with Middle Gujarati

During the transition towards Middle Gujarati, characteristic grammatical forms became increasingly established. These included the auxiliary stem represented in Modern Gujarati by chhe and the possessive marker represented by forms such as no, ni and nu.

Gujarati also acquired vocabulary through interaction with Persian and Arabic during the medieval period. This influence was particularly important in administration, commerce and the speech of certain communities.

Authors such as Akho, Premanand and Dayaram continued to broaden the literary functions of Gujarati through philosophical, narrative and devotional compositions. Their works helped transmit the language across generations and social groups.

Prelims focus

  • Acharya Hemachandra is associated with Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana.
  • Hemachandra received patronage during the Solanki period.
  • Shalibhadra Suri composed Bharateshwar Bahubali Ras in 1185 CE.
  • Narsinh Mehta is traditionally honoured as Adikavi.
  • Bhalan is associated with the expression Gurjar Bhakha.
  • Trap: Early Jain compositions existed before Narsinh Mehta.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 7, English edition 2021–22, Chapter 8, Formation of Regional Culture, p. 41; Social Science, Standard 10, English edition, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, pp. 31–32; NCERT, Our Pasts II, Class 7, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, pp. 109 and 114–115; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Gujarat: Gujarati Language and Literature, sections on early Gujarati and literary history; The Emergence of Hindi Literature, Oxford University Research Archive, p. 9, discussion of Maru-Gurjar literature; Neo-Brahmi Generation Panel, Proposal for a Gujarati Script Root Zone Label Generation Ruleset, 2019, pp. 3–4. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Old and Middle Gujarati: Grammarians, Manuscripts and Literary Development

body:
The expansion of Modern Gujarati

The development of Modern Gujarati accelerated during the 19th century. Although Gujarati already possessed a substantial literary tradition, printing and formal education enabled it to serve a much wider range of functions.

Gujarati increasingly became a medium for newspapers, textbooks, essays, novels, administrative communication and public discussion. The growth of prose was especially significant because it expanded the use of Gujarati beyond poetry, religious compositions and traditional narratives.

Printing and the Gujarati press

The introduction of printing allowed large numbers of readers to access identical copies of a text. Printed publications gradually encouraged greater consistency in spelling, punctuation and written expression.

Fardunjee Marzban, a Parsi printer and journalist associated with Surat and Bombay, was a pioneer of Gujarati printing and journalism. He established a Gujarati printing press in Bombay in 1812.

On 1 July 1822, he began publishing the Gujarati newspaper that became known as Bombay Samachar, now Mumbai Samachar. It initially appeared as a weekly publication.

The development of Gujarati journalism made the language increasingly important for commercial information, public affairs and social reform. The contribution of the Parsi community to early Gujarati printing demonstrates that the language developed through the participation of different communities.

Narmad and Gujarati lexicography

Lexicography is the preparation and compilation of dictionaries. Dictionaries help establish accepted spellings, record word meanings and document the vocabulary of a language.

Narmadashankar Lalshankar Dave, popularly known as Narmad, was an important figure in the development of Modern Gujarati. He compiled Narmakosh, a pioneering Gujarati dictionary whose comprehensive edition was published at Surat in 1873.

Narmakosh is particularly important as an early monolingual Gujarati dictionary. A monolingual dictionary explains words using the same language, whereas a bilingual dictionary provides meanings or equivalents in another language.

Narmad's contribution therefore extended beyond poetry and literature to the systematic recording of Gujarati vocabulary.

Gujarat Vidyapith and spelling standardisation

Standardisation is the development and acceptance of common conventions for the formal use of a language. It includes agreement on spelling, grammatical usage and other written conventions.

Gujarat Vidyapith established its Kosh Karyalay in Ahmedabad in 1929 at the suggestion of Mahatma Gandhi. It published the first edition of Sarth Gujarati Jodanikosh in the same year.

The original edition recorded accepted spellings. The second edition, published in 1931, added word meanings. The dictionary became an important resource for consistency in written Gujarati.

Narmakosh is primarily associated with Narmad's contribution to Gujarati lexicography. Sarth Gujarati Jodanikosh is particularly associated with spelling standardisation through Gujarat Vidyapith.

The development of Standard Gujarati

The development of a common written standard was influenced substantially by the speech of central Gujarat, particularly the Ahmedabad–Vadodara region. Schools, dictionaries, textbooks, newspapers and literary institutions helped spread the standard form.

Standard Gujarati provides a shared medium for people from different dialect regions. Its adoption in formal communication does not require speakers to abandon the regional or community varieties they use in their everyday lives.

Prelims focus

  • Fardunjee Marzban established a Gujarati printing press in Bombay in 1812.
  • Bombay Samachar began publication on 1 July 1822.
  • Narmakosh was compiled by Narmadashankar Lalshankar Dave.
  • The comprehensive edition of Narmakosh was published in 1873.
  • Gujarat Vidyapith published the first Jodanikosh in 1929.
  • The 1931 edition of Jodanikosh included word meanings.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English edition, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, p. 31; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook, Surat, Part A, Analytical Note, entry on Fardoonji Marzban; Press Information Bureau, Dwishatabdi Mahotsav of Mumbai Samachar, 12 June 2022; Gujarati Sahitya Parishad, Narmadashankar Dave, author profile and list of works; Granth Sanjeevani, Narmakosh, bibliographic record of the 1873 Surat edition; Gujarat Vidyapith, Kosh Karyalay, Editions of Sarth Gujarati Jodni Kosh; George Cardona, A Gujarati Reference Grammar, Introduction. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]
